title: Fix the protected-argument check in `blackboost_train()`
description:

```r
other_args <- other_args[
```

title: predict() fails for coxph fits with several variables in one strata() term
description:
Predicting from a `proportional_hazards()` fit with the `"survival"` engine fails
whenever a single `strata()` term contains more than one variable — even though
both stratification variables are present in `new_data`.

```r
library(censored)

lung2 <- na.omit(lung[, c("time", "status", "age", "sex", "ph.ecog")])

cph_fit <- proportional_hazards() |>
  set_engine("survival") |>
  set_mode("censored regression") |>
  fit(Surv(time, status) ~ age + strata(sex, ph.ecog), data = lung2)

names(lung2)
#> [1] "time"    "status"  "age"     "sex"     "ph.ecog"

predict(cph_fit, lung2[1:3, ], type = "time")
#> Error in `predict_time()`:
#> ! `new_data` is missing the following stratification variable: `sex, ph.ecog`.
```

Note the error names a single "variable" called `sex, ph.ecog`, which is the
giveaway: the two variable names have not been separated.

`fit()` itself is fine — the underlying `coxph` fit has the expected strata. Only
prediction is affected, and both `type = "time"` and `type = "survival"` fail,
since they share the same `pre` hook.

What triggers it:

| formula | `predict()` |
|---|---|
| `~ age + strata(sex)` | works |
| `~ age + strata(sex) + strata(ph.ecog)` | works |
| `~ age + strata(sex, ph.ecog)` | **fails** |

The multi-variable form is documented as valid elsewhere in the package —
`check_strata_nterms()` tells users to write exactly this when they need several
strata columns with `glmnet`:

> It can contain multiple strata columns, e.g., `~ x + strata(s1, s2)`.

and it works on the `glmnet` engine.

### Cause

`cph_survival_pre()` in `R/proportional_hazards-survival.R` recovers the strata
variable names by string surgery on the term labels:

```r
strata <- attr(terms_x, "term.labels")
strata <- grep(pattern = "^strata", x = strata, value = TRUE)
strata <- sub(pattern = "strata\\(", replacement = "", x = strata)
strata <- sub(pattern = "\\)", replacement = "", x = strata)
strata_available <- strata %in% names(new_data)
```

For `strata(sex, ph.ecog)` the term label is the single string
`"strata(sex, ph.ecog)"`, so this yields the one element `"sex, ph.ecog"`, which
can never match a column name. Two *separate* terms work only because they happen
to give one label each.

### Suggested fix

Take the names from the `specials` attribute rather than from the printed term
labels:

```r
strata_ind <- attr(terms_x, "specials")$strata
strata_calls <- attr(terms_x, "variables")[strata_ind + 1]
strata <- unlist(lapply(strata_calls, all.vars))
```

(The `+ 1` is because `attr(terms, "variables")[[1]]` is the `list` call itself.)
This returns the right names for all three formula shapes above — `sex`;
`sex`, `ph.ecog`; and `sex`, `ph.ecog` respectively — and it also fixes the
message's pluralization for free, since the vector now has one element per
variable.

`survival::untangle.specials(terms_x, "strata", 1)$vars` is the neighbouring
option, but it returns the *wrapped* names (`"strata(sex, ph.ecog)"`), so it would
still need `all.vars()` on top.

### Tests

- Add a test that `predict()` succeeds for a `strata(s1, s2)` fit when both
  columns are in `new_data`, and errors naming **both** variables when they are
  absent.
- The existing snapshots in "prediction from stratified models require strata
  variables in new_data" (`tests/testthat/test-proportional_hazards-survival.R`)
  must be unchanged — a genuinely missing single strata variable still has to
  error with `` `new_data` is missing the following stratification variable:
  `inst`. ``, which I confirmed the suggested fix preserves.

title: `bag_tree()` with the `"rpart"` engine silently ignores case weights
description:
## Summary

`bag_tree()` / `"rpart"` (censored regression, via `ipred::bagging()`) is
registered as supporting case weights (`"weights"` is in the `protect` list of
its `set_fit()` registration), but the weights have no effect on the fit. A
weighted fit that zero-weights half the rows produces the same trees and the
same predictions as the unweighted fit.

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(censored)
#> Loading required package: parsnip
#> Loading required package: survival
library(survival)

data("time_to_million", package = "censored")
df <- time_to_million[1:100, c("time", "event", "released_theaters", "rated")]

# Importance weights that drop the first 50 rows entirely (weight 0).
wts <- importance_weights(c(rep(0, 50), rep(1, 50)))

spec <- bag_tree() |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("censored regression")

set.seed(1)
wt_fit <- fit(spec, Surv(time, event) ~ ., data = df, case_weights = wts)
set.seed(1)
unwt_fit <- fit(spec, Surv(time, event) ~ ., data = df)

# The bagged trees are equal even though half the data was zero-weighted
all.equal(wt_fit$fit$mtrees, unwt_fit$fit$mtrees)
#> [1] TRUE

# ... and so are the predictions: the case weights had no effect
all.equal(
  predict(wt_fit, df, type = "time"),
  predict(unwt_fit, df, type = "time")
)
#> [1] TRUE
```

## Root cause

`bag_tree` / `"rpart"` is registered (`R/bag_tree-data.R`) with
`protect = c("formula", "data", "weights")` and `func = ipred::bagging`.
`bagging()` dispatches to `ipred:::ipredbagg.Surv(y, X, nbagg, control, comb,
coob, ns, keepX, ...)`, which has no `weights` argument — the `weights` passed
by parsnip fall into `...` and are dropped by the bootstrap resampling. So the
weights never influence the fit.

## Suggested resolution

Either wire the weights into the bagged fit properly (if `ipred` can honor
them), or, if weighted bagging is not supported, remove `"weights"` from the
`protect` list so parsnip reports the engine as not accepting case weights
instead of silently ignoring them.

title: `null_model()` with the `"survival"` engine errors when given case weights
description:
## Summary

Fitting a `null_model()` with the `"survival"` engine (censored regression)
errors as soon as `case_weights` are supplied, even though the engine is
registered as supporting weights and `survival::survfit()` handles weights on
the same data without issue.

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(censored)
#> Loading required package: parsnip
#> Loading required package: survival
library(survival)

spec <- null_model() |>
  set_engine("survival") |>
  set_mode("censored regression")

set.seed(1)
wts <- importance_weights(runif(nrow(lung)))

# Fitting a null model with case weights errors:
fit(spec, Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = lung, case_weights = wts)
#> Error:
#> ! ..1 used in an incorrect context, no ... to look in

# ... even though survival::survfit() handles weights on the same data fine:
km <- survival::survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung, weights = runif(nrow(lung)))
class(km)
#> [1] "survfit"
```

## Root cause

The engine's fit wrapper (`R/null_model-survival.R`) is:

```r
survfit_null <- function(formula, data, ...) {
  formula <- stats::update(formula, . ~ 1)
  survival::survfit(formula, data = data, ...)
}
```

parsnip passes `weights` through `...`. `survival::survfit.formula()`
re-evaluates its `weights` argument inside `model.frame()`, but because the
`weights` expression arrives via `...` (and the formula has been rebuilt by
`update()`), that evaluation fails with `..1 used in an incorrect context, no
... to look in`. Passing `weights` positionally/by name to `survfit()` instead
of forwarding it through `...` avoids the non-standard-evaluation problem.

## Suggested resolution

Give `survfit_null()` an explicit `weights` argument and pass it directly to
`survival::survfit()` (rather than relying on `...`), so weighted null models
fit and produce a weighted Kaplan-Meier curve.

title: `survival_reg()` (survival engine): NA in a strata variable yields a wrong, non-NA prediction
description:
Found this while increasing test coverage for `survival_reg(engine = "survival")`

## Summary

When a fitted `survival_reg()` model uses `strata()` (so `survival::survreg()`
estimates one scale per stratum) and `new_data` contains a row with a **missing
value in the strata variable**, the survival/hazard prediction for that row is
**not `NA`**. Instead it silently uses some *other* stratum's scale — and which
one depends on the rest of `new_data`. Only when every stratum happens to be
present in `new_data` does the missing-strata row correctly return `NA`.

This violates the row contract (NA in → NA out, rows preserved) and produces
plausible-looking but wrong numbers.

## Expected behaviour

A row with `NA` in the strata variable should predict `NA`, regardless of what
other rows are in `new_data`.

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(censored)
#> Loading required package: parsnip
#> Loading required package: survival
library(survival)

# A parametric survival model with a stratified scale: survreg() estimates
# one scale per stratum of `sex`.
mod <- survival_reg() |>
  set_engine("survival") |>
  fit(Surv(time, status) ~ age + strata(sex), data = lung)

extract_fit_engine(mod)$scale
#>     sex=1     sex=2 
#> 0.8096431 0.6627983

# Build new data whose first row has a *missing* strata value (`sex`).
# The remaining rows control which strata are present in `new_data`.
na_and_sex1 <- lung[c(1, 2), ] # rows 1, 2 are both sex = 1
na_and_sex1$sex[1] <- NA

na_and_sex2 <- lung[c(1, 7), ] # row 7 is sex = 2
na_and_sex2$sex[1] <- NA

na_and_both <- lung[c(1, 2, 7), ] # both strata present
na_and_both$sex[1] <- NA

# Predicted survival for the NA-strata row (row 1) in each case.
# Expectation (vctrs row contract): NA in -> NA out, always.
predict(mod, na_and_sex1, type = "survival", eval_time = 100)$.pred[[1]]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   .eval_time .pred_survival
#>        <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1        100          0.871
predict(mod, na_and_sex2, type = "survival", eval_time = 100)$.pred[[1]]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   .eval_time .pred_survival
#>        <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1        100          0.820
predict(mod, na_and_both, type = "survival", eval_time = 100)$.pred[[1]]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   .eval_time .pred_survival
#>        <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1        100             NA

# The internal scale lookup shows what is going wrong: the NA-strata row is
# assigned whichever stratum's scale is *absent* from new_data.
censored:::get_survreg_scale(extract_fit_engine(mod), na_and_sex1)
#> [1] 0.6627983 0.8096431
censored:::get_survreg_scale(extract_fit_engine(mod), na_and_sex2)
#> [1] 0.8096431 0.6627983
censored:::get_survreg_scale(extract_fit_engine(mod), na_and_both)
#> [1]        NA 0.8096431 0.6627983
```

The NA-strata row (row 1, originally `sex = 1`) is assigned:

- the `sex=2` scale when the only other stratum present is `sex=1`,
- the `sex=1` scale when the only other stratum present is `sex=2`,
- `NA` only when both strata appear in `new_data`.

Both `type = "survival"` and `type = "hazard"` are affected, via
`survival_prob_survreg()` and `hazard_survreg()`.

## Root cause

`deparse_survreg_strata()` in `R/survival_reg-survival.R`:

```r
deparse_survreg_strata <- function(object, new_data) {
  new_new_data <- compute_strata(object, new_data)
  lvls <- levels(new_new_data$.strata)

  # link this to scales vector
  scales <- tibble(.strata = names(object$scale), .scale = unname(object$scale))
  scales$.strata <- factor(scales$.strata, levels = lvls)

  # return a vector with appropriate estimates for new data
  new_new_data$.row <- seq_len(nrow(new_new_data))
  new_new_data <- dplyr::left_join(new_new_data, scales, by = ".strata")
  new_new_data <- new_new_data[order(new_new_data$.row), ]
  new_new_data$.scale
}
```

`lvls` is taken from the strata that appear in `new_data`. The line
`scales$.strata <- factor(scales$.strata, levels = lvls)` then coerces the name
of any stratum *not* present in `new_data` to `NA`. A `new_data` row whose
strata value is missing also has `.strata == NA`, so the subsequent
`dplyr::left_join(by = ".strata")` matches that row to the `NA`-keyed scale row
— i.e. it picks up the scale of whichever stratum was absent from `new_data`.
When no stratum is absent (all present), there is no `NA`-keyed scale row, so
the join yields `NA` (the only case that happens to be correct).

## Suggested fix direction

Match scales to strata by the stratum name/level rather than by a factor whose
levels depend on `new_data`, and let a genuinely missing strata value map to
`NA`. A missing `.strata` in `new_data` should always produce `NA` scale →
`NA` prediction, independent of `new_data` composition.

title: Time predictions from `decision_tree()` with the "rpart" engine correct?
description:
When I run decision_tree() with the "rpart" engine, I see that the results of the tune() function's concordance index and also the calculation on a test sample give results less than 0.5, when I expect them to be greater than 0.5. I provide an example with a well-known survival data file (Hosmer), extracted from the "smoothHR" package.
I have tested with other files and the results are similar. Also, if I repeat this script changing the engine to "partykit", I get a concordance index greater than 0.7, which is correct.

```r
library(tidymodels)
library(censored)
library(smoothHR)

## Data
whas500 <- whas500 %>% select(age, gender, hr, sysbp, diasbp, bmi, cvd, afb,
                              sho, chf, av3, miord, mitype, lenfol, fstat)

set.seed(252)
whas500_split <- initial_split(whas500, strata = fstat)
whas500_train <- training(whas500_split)
whas500_test <- testing(whas500_split)
                         
whas500_train <- whas500_train %>%
  mutate(surv_var = Surv(lenfol, fstat), .keep = "unused")
whas500_test <- whas500_test %>%
  mutate(surv_var = Surv(lenfol, fstat), .keep = "unused")

## resampling
set.seed(253)
cv_split <- vfold_cv(whas500_train, v = 10, repeats = 2 )

## Model specification
tree_spec <- 
    decision_tree( tree_depth = tune(), min_n = tune(),
                   cost_complexity = tune() ) %>%
    set_engine("rpart") %>% 
    set_mode("censored regression") 
              
## Workflow              
wflow_tree <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(tree_spec) %>% 
  add_formula(surv_var ~ . ) 
  
## Parameters Tune
tree_grid <- grid_regular(cost_complexity(), tree_depth(), min_n(),
                          levels = 4 )    

tune_result_tree <- wflow_tree %>% 
  tune_grid( resamples = cv_split, grid = tree_grid, 
             metrics = metric_set(concordance_survival) ) 
show_best(tune_result_tree, metric="concordance_survival")

## Final workflow and final mpdel
final_wflow_tree <- wflow_tree %>% 
  finalize_workflow( select_best(tune_result_tree, metric="concordance_survival") )
tree_fit <- final_wflow_tree %>% fit(whas500_train)
tree_fit

## Predictions in the testing sample
pred_tree_time <- predict(tree_fit, whas500_test, type = "time")
pred_tree_df <- bind_cols(whas500_test %>% select(surv_var), pred_tree_time ) 
head(pred_tree_df)

## Concordance
concordance_survival(pred_tree_df, truth = surv_var, estimate = .pred_time ) 


```

title: `coxnet_train()` struggles with large number of predictors
description:
Originally surfaced in https://community.rstudio.com/t/error-with-tuning-for-censored-regression/181248, here is a more minimal reprex.

``` r
library(censored)
#> Loading required package: parsnip
#> Loading required package: survival

set.seed(1)
lung <- na.omit(lung)
surv <- Surv(lung$time[1:125], lung$status[1:125])
predictors <- matrix(runif(n = 125 * 22215), nrow = 125)

dat <- cbind(
  data.frame(surv = surv),
  as.data.frame(predictors)
)

# pure glmnet model works
glmnet_fit <- glmnet::glmnet(x = as.matrix(dat[, -1]), y = dat$surv, family = "cox")

# single parsnip model fails
parsnip_fit <- fit(proportional_hazards(engine = "glmnet", penalty = 0.1), surv ~ ., data = dat)
#> Error: protect(): protection stack overflow

# reducing the number of predictors makes it work again
parsnip_fit <- fit(proportional_hazards(engine = "glmnet", penalty = 0.1), surv ~ ., data = dat[, 1:16500])
```

```r
      truth, estimate, case_weights

    }

}

  length(x[[1]]$.eval_time)
}

roc_auc_survival_integrated_impl <- function(truth,
                                             estimate,
                                             case_weights) {

    truth = truth,
    estimate = estimate,
    na_rm = FALSE,
    case_weights = case_weights
  )
  
  n <- length(res$.estimate)
  sum(diff(res$.eval_time) * (res$.estimate[1:(n - 1)] + res$.estimate[2:n]) / 2) / max(res$.eval_time)
```

title: survival 3.7-0 breaks censored
description:
The new version of survival allows for infinite evaluation time points in the summary method for survfit objects instead of omitting them. It also now preserves the order of the time points.

censored captured those time points (and their order) and returned survival probabilities 1 and 0 for eval times of -Inf and Inf, respectively. We can depend on the new version of survival and remove our own handling of these cases.

## With survival 3.7-0

``` r
library(survival)
library(glmnet)
#> Loading required package: Matrix
#> Loaded glmnet 4.1-8

pred_time <- c(1022, -Inf, 0, Inf, 1022, -Inf)

# for coxph
lung_pred <- tidyr::drop_na(lung)
mod <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = lung)
surv_fit <- survfit(mod, newdata = lung_pred[1:2, ])
summary(surv_fit, times = pred_time, extend = TRUE)
#> Call: survfit(formula = mod, newdata = lung_pred[1:2, ])
#> 
#>  time n.risk n.event survival1 survival2
#>  1022      1       0     0.117   0.00158
#>  -Inf    167       0     1.000   1.00000
#>     0    167       0     1.000   1.00000
#>   Inf      0       0     0.117   0.00158
#>  1022      1       0     0.117   0.00158
#>  -Inf    167       0     1.000   1.00000

# for general survfit
lung2 <- lung[-14, ]
lung_x <- as.matrix(lung2[, c("age", "ph.ecog")])
lung_y <- Surv(lung2$time, lung2$status)
lung_pred <- lung_x[1:2, ]

  glmnet::glmnet(x = lung_x, y = lung_y, family = "cox")

surv_fit <- survfit(mod, newx = lung_pred, s = 0.1, x = lung_x, y = lung_y)
```

title: Harmonize input for `survival_prob_*()` and `surival_time_*()` functions
description:
The `survival_prob_*()` and `surival_time_*()` functions typically take a model object as fitted by the engine as input. The exceptions are the two functions for glmnet objects (coxnet), which need the parsnip `model_fit` object (for some additional components that are not stored in the engine fit object directly).

These functions preferably all take the same input object. Since we do need the parsnip fit for glmnet, we'd need to change all the other functions.  This would be a breaking change. They are technically exported but developer-facing and tagged with `@keyword internal`. 

I think it makes sense to bite the bullet now and introduce that breaking change: Those functions are not advertised as user-facing, censored is still in its experimental lifecycle stage, we are still "before the big release cascade" for survival analysis, and we might have to live with this rather big inconsistency for rather long.

There is currently some code in `aaa_survival_prop.R` to estimate survival probabilities for Cox PH models. It might be better to use `survift(coxph_object)` or `basehaz(coxph_object)` to get these since they take into account any stratification variables for that model. Dealing with the strata is a pain, because of how `survival` encodes them, but some of that work is already done for the parametric model engine. 

Also, I don't see any canonical ways of estimating the baseline hazard so that we can get `type = "hazard"`. There as some methods that layer another model on top of the PH model results. It would be good to get community feedback on this. 

We might also consider having a `type = "cumulative hazard"` method

description:
With `glmnet` (and maybe `mboost`) we can get predictions one many values of some tuning parameters without multiple model fits. `parsnip` saves those as nested tibbles per row of `new_data`.

title: Support spline-based distribution for flexsurv
description:
## Feature

I posted this over on the [RStudio Community forum](https://community.rstudio.com/t/feedback-on-the-censored-package-for-survival-analysis-with-tidymodels/119674/14?u=mattwarkentin), but I thought it might be easier to track/discuss over here, so I will copy and paste the post.

> Oh and while I'm thinking of it, I would suggest supporting flexsurv::flexsurvspline() in addition to flexsurv::flexsurvreg() for survival_reg(). The latter is based on known parametric distributions (e.g. Weibull, etc.), while the former supports arbitrarily flexible baseline (cumulative) hazards with natural cubic splines (Royston-Parmar model).

> Maybe some sentinel function like dist_spline(k, knots, bknots, scale = 'hazard', timescale = 'log') that defines the spline model, where k is mutually exclusive with knots/bknots. An API like:

```r
survival_reg(engine = 'flexsurv', dist = dist_spline(k = tune()))
```
> This might require adding a dials::knots() function, which would be very similar to the dials::deg_free() function.

For the case weights branch in parsnip, there is an error with glmnet and Cox models. 

``` r
library(survival)

    set_engine("glmnet", nlambda = 5) %>%
```

title: Missing values when getting survival probabilities for coxnet models
description:
This issue is about how the `survfit()` method for `coxnet` models handles missing values. There is a corresponding issue #40 for `coxph` models.

We would like results of `survfit()` to be padded for observations with missing values, however, `na.exclude()` does not do this consistently, it depends on the penalty.

``` r
library(survival)
library(glmnet)
#> Loading required package: Matrix
#> Loaded glmnet 4.1-1

# prep and fit non-stratified and stratified model
lung2 <- lung[-14,] # includes NA, glmnet doesn't fit with NA
lung_x <- as.matrix(lung2[, c("age", "ph.ecog")])
lung_y <- Surv(lung2$time, lung2$status)
fit_glmnet <- glmnet(lung_x, lung_y, family = "cox")
lung_y_s <- stratifySurv(lung_y, lung2$sex)
fit_glmnet_s <- glmnet(lung_x, lung_y_s, family = "cox")
#> Warning: cox.fit: algorithm did not converge

# non-stratified
new_x <- as.matrix(lung[14:16, c("age", "ph.ecog")])
sf <- survfit(fit_glmnet, newx = new_x, x = lung_x, y = lung_y,
              na.action = na.exclude)

# includes all 3 observations
sf[[1]] 
#> Call: survfit.coxnet(formula = fit_glmnet, newx = new_x, x = lung_x, 
#>     y = lung_y, na.action = na.exclude)
#> 
#>      n events median
#> 14 227    164    310
#> 15 227    164    310
#> 16 227    164    310

# includes only 2
sf[[2]] 
#> Call: survfit.coxnet(formula = fit_glmnet, newx = new_x, x = lung_x, 
#>     y = lung_y, na.action = na.exclude)
#> 
#>      n events median
#> 15 227    164    310
#> 16 227    164    310

# stratified
new_x <- as.matrix(lung[14:16, c("age", "ph.ecog")])
new_strata <- as.matrix(lung[14:16, "sex", drop = FALSE])
sf_s <- survfit(fit_glmnet_s, newx = new_x, newstrata = new_strata,

# includes all 3 observations

#> Call: survfit.coxnet(formula = fit_glmnet_s, newx = new_x, newstrata = new_strata,
```

title: workflows::add_formula doesn't work with censored
description:
## The problem

I'm trying to integrate censored into an existing project, where it is important to refit data without passing the formula to the fit argument. This can usually be achieved with `workflows::add_formula()`, after which we can fit by only specifying the workflow and data. 

However, apparently, `add_formula()` is ignored and I get an error notifying me I must use the formula interface.

``` r
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip

#> Loading required package: survival

lung <- lung %>% drop_na()
ph_spec <- 
  proportional_hazards() %>%
  set_engine("survival") %>% 
  set_mode("censored regression")

ph_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(ph_spec) %>%
  add_formula(Surv(time, status) ~ .)
ph_workflow

#>

ph_fit <- ph_workflow %>% fit(data = lung)
```

title: Interval-censored Cox proportional hazards models
description:
Thank you for this package, it is exciting to see its rapid development.

Stata 17 added support for interval-censored semiparametric Cox proportional hazards models in the [stintcox](https://www.stata.com/manuals/ststintcox.pdf) function. with interval-censored data. Biometrika 103: 253–271. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/asw013

title: Multiple survival curves for single observation from stratified survival model
description:
For a stratified Cox model, `survival::survfit()` should return a single survival curve per observation if the strata information is given in the `newdata` arg. If no information on the strata is given, it returns a curve for each stratum. This works as intended for `newdata` data frame which contain multiple observations, however if `newdata` only contains a single observation, `survfit()` returns a curve per stratum, even if the information for the stratum is given in `newdata`.

``` r
library(survival)

cfit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + wt.loss + strata(inst),
              data = lung)

# no strata info --> survival curves for all strata
new_data_0 <- expand.grid(age = c(50, 60), sex = 1, wt.loss = 5)
csurv_0 <- survfit(cfit, newdata = new_data_0)
dim(csurv_0)
#> strata   data
#>     18      2

# add strata info --> survival curves for only those
new_data_n <- data.frame(age = c(50, 60), sex = 1:2, wt.loss = 5, inst = c(6, 11))
csurv_n <- survfit(cfit, newdata = new_data_n)
dim(csurv_n)
#> strata
#>      2

# single observation with strata info --> should be one curve but gives all
new_data_1 <- data.frame(age = 60, sex = 2, wt.loss = 5, inst = 11)
csurv_1 <- survfit(cfit, newdata = new_data_1)
dim(csurv_1)
#> strata
#>     18
```

title: Is there a way to incorporate confidence interval or prediction interval when making predictions for coxph?
description:
In traditional `coxph` approach, there is a way of including `se.fit = TRUE` to get the standard errors and then calculate confidence intervals based on the s.e.. However, I don't think I found a way to do this in the parsnip approach. See the following example.

```
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, tidymodels, survival, data.table, survival, censored)

heart = read.csv('http://s3.amazonaws.com/h2o-public-test-data/smalldata/coxph_test/heart.csv') %>% 
  mutate(t2event = stop - start)

# Traditional coxph approach works for getting se
fit_coxph = coxph(Surv(t2event, event) ~ age + surgery + transplant, data = heart)

heart = heart %>% 
  mutate(
    pred_expected = predict(
      fit_coxph,
      newdata = .,
      type = 'survival',
      se.fit = TRUE
    )$fit,
    pred_expected_se = predict(
      fit_coxph,
      newdata = .,
      type = 'survival',
      se.fit = TRUE
    )$se.fit
  )


# Fitting a parsnip object
fit_cox_tidymodel =
  proportional_hazards() %>%
  set_engine("survival") %>% 
  fit(Surv(t2event, event) ~ age + surgery + transplant,
      data = heart)

time_vec = seq(0, max(heart$t2event), 1)

heart %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  mutate(
    predict(
      fit_cox_tidymodel,
      new_data = .,
      type = 'survival',
      time = time_vec
    ),
    # parsnip does not seem to work for getting se
    predict(fit_cox_tidymodel,
            new_data = .,
            type = 'pred_int',
            time = time_vec)
```

title: survival probabilities for glmnet proportional hazards model
description:
We want to get survival probabilities for `glmnet` objects that use `family = "cox"`.  [This page](https://glmnet.stanford.edu/articles/Coxnet.html) has details on the Cox model with `glmnet` and describes the special approach that is required for this model implementation. 

There are a few complications that arise when building a wrapper around this model: 

## No formulas

`glmnet()` does *not* use a formula method so something simple like `Surv(time, event) ~ x_1 + x_2` isn't possible. In [their examples](https://glmnet.stanford.edu/articles/Coxnet.html#basic-usage-for-right-censored-data-1), they has the contents of the `Surv()` object as a matrix (or an object of class `Surv`) to the `glmnet()` function. I believe that the `censored` package already deals with this.

The main consequence of no formula method is that, for stratification, we cannot use the canonical function (e.g., `Surv(time, event) ~ x_1 + x_2 + strata(var)`). There is a different function that is used on the *outcome* object to store the stratification variable. The syntax looks like `stratifySurv(surv_object, strata_var)`.

## Retain the training set

Like the `survival` package, survival probabilities for the Cox model are best computed by using the `survfit()` method on the model object. While `glmnet` _does_ have a `survfit()` method for their data, it requires the original training set data to work.

We'll have to attach `x` and `y` data to the fitted `glmnet` object when the model is fit.

## Predictions over penalty values

Like other `glmnet` objects, we can make predictions over many values of `lambda` for the same model object. For survival probabilities, this is also the case. When making such predictions, we also need to specify the time points. As a result, the standard nested tibble that `censored` produces will have a row for each combination of `.time` and `lambda` and would look something like:

    # A tibble: 4 x 3
      .time .pred_survival penalty
      <dbl>          <dbl>   <dbl>
    1     1          0.966    0.01
    2    10          0.448    0.01
    3     1          0.951    0.1 
    4    10          0.421    0.1 

The initial work here is to make a function similar to `censored::cph_survival_prob()` to get the data in this format. It looks like `survival:::survfit.coxph()` produces a list of `survfit` objects for each value of `lambda`. It may not bee too complex to get these predictions and then reformat them (which we have code to do for the results of `survival:::survfit.coxph()`).

**Note**: [recall](https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/issues/195) that, when a `glmnet` model is fit via `parsnip`, we require a single penalty value (even though the model produces all of the coefficients for the entire path of penalty values). For this reason, `predict.model_fit()` will only produce predictions for a single penalty value. This function should produce the above output *without the penalty column*. The `multi_predict()` method will have an argument for the penalty values and its results will look like the tibble above.

title: improve `multi_predict()`
description:
Rather than relying on the name/`.id` behavior in `map_dfr()`, you might consider doing `map2_dfr(y, penalty, ~stack_survfit(.x, n = nrow(new_data), penalty = .y))`.

You could have this signature `stack_survfit(x, n, penalty = NULL)` and just unconditionally add the penalty column to the front of the tibbles you create. `tibble()` will automatically drop `NULL` columns, and will recycle `penalty` of size 1 as required.

```r
library(tibble)
tibble(penalty = NULL, y = 1:2)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>       y
#>   <int>
#> 1     1
#> 2     2
tibble(penalty = 0.01, y = 1:2)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   penalty     y
#>     <dbl> <int>
#> 1    0.01     1
#> 2    0.01     2
```

_Originally posted by @DavisVaughan in https://github.com/tidymodels/censored/pull/70#discussion_r661604766_

title: Include MTLR model for direct estimation of survival probabilities and supporting feature effects varying over time
description:
## Feature

Hi there, this is a hugely welcome addition to the R stack for the pharma community! Thanks so much for working on this.

Apart from the issues which are still on your [ToDo list](https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2021/11/survival-analysis-parsnip-adjacent/), I would like to highlight a particular model which has been shown to work very well in benchmarks as well as in practice, Multi-task Logistic Regression (MTLR). 

The approach is originally from [NIPS 2011](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2011/hash/1019c8091693ef5c5f55970346633f92-Abstract.html) and already available on [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/MTLR/) by @haiderstats; it's prediction modes are displayed in the [Vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/MTLR/vignettes/workflow.html). The package is actively maintained on [Github](https://github.com/haiderstats/MTLR). There is a [very detailed Rmd](https://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/437544_1feb48fe03234a3abecf81726c1c3905.html) by the package author that compares different R models for estimating per-patient survival probabilities.

The following resources contain the original paper and subsequent benchmarks and applications; MTLR does very well in the benchmarks:

- [2011 NeurIPS paper](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2011/hash/1019c8091693ef5c5f55970346633f92-Abstract.html)
- [2018 ArXiv paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.11347)
- [2019 master thesis by the package author](https://www.caiac.ca/sites/default/files/publications/Haider-MSc-Thesis.pdf)
- [2020 JMLR paper](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v21/18-772.html)
- [Benchmark R code for 2020 JMLR paper (maybe a good dataset to include in tidymodels?)](https://github.com/haiderstats/ISDEvaluation)
- [2020 BMC application paper](https://d-nb.info/1169646484/34)
- [2020 AAI application paper](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7963212/)
- [2021 PMLR benchmark paper](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8232898/)
- [2021 ArXiv paper for SurvBenchmark (including a large benchmarking dataset and comparison of 20 methods)](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.07.11.451967v2)
- [SurvBenchmark R package GitHub repo](https://github.com/yunwezhang/SurvBenchmark_package)
- [SurvBenchmark benchmark code for paper GitHub repo](https://github.com/SydneyBioX/SurvBenchmark)

The methods's main advantages are that it provides *per-patient* survival probabilities (i.e., it predicts the survival function itself) across a range of times (i.e., it allows for feature effects to vary through time). Also, it works with many different forms of censoring events, which makes it very versatile (although it still does not allow for missing values, unfortunately).

To quote from the R package vignette:

> MTLR was specifically designed to give **survival probabilities** across a **range of times** for **individual observations** . This differs from models which produce risk scores (such as those given by Cox proportional hazards), single time probability models (such as the Gail model), and population wide models ( *e.g.* Kaplan-Meier curves). Producing survival probabilities over a range of times gives a more holistic view of survival to patients and physicians which may be critical in making healthcare decisions.

> MTLR can be used for survival data containing right, left, interval, or no censoring. In addition, these types of censoring can be mixed in the same dataset.

(I am not involved with any of these papers nor do I know the authors of the papers or the package maintainer)
